title: The Tax You Already Paid and Never Claimed Back: Input Tax Recovery on Employee Expenses
summary: GST and VAT on employee expense claims is routinely unrecovered because coding is wrong or evidence is invalid. Here's how to recover it systematically.
body_markdown:
**💡 TL;DR**


Every employee expense claim carries tax your business may be entitled to recover — and in most organisations a large share of it is never claimed. Not because of aggressive blocked-category rules, but because of three mundane failures: claims **coded gross with no tax split** , **card slips submitted instead of tax invoices** , and **blanket conservative coding** where finance marks everything non-recoverable rather than assessing each claim. All three are data problems with data fixes. The recoverable amount is real cash, and it is currently sitting in your expense line.


---


## The Line Item Nobody Audits


Finance teams scrutinise T&E spend constantly. Limits, approvals, duplicate claims, policy exceptions — all of it gets attention.


The tax sitting inside that spend gets almost none.


Ask a controller how much recoverable GST or VAT was claimed back on employee expense claims last quarter, and the answer is usually a pause. The number exists somewhere in the return, aggregated with everything else, and nobody has ever separated the T&E component to see whether it looks right.


This is understandable. Input tax on expense claims is small per transaction, spread across thousands of claims, and governed by rules that vary by category and jurisdiction. Getting it right on a single S$120 restaurant receipt returns a few dollars. The effort-to-value ratio on any individual claim is terrible.


Which is exactly why it is worth automating rather than ignoring. The per-claim value is trivial and the aggregate is not — and unlike most finance improvements, this one produces actual cash rather than avoided cost.


---


## Why Recoverable Tax Goes Unrecovered


Three failures account for most of the gap, and none of them is about tax law being complicated.


### 1. The claim is coded gross


An employee submits a claim for S$128.40. That number goes into the system, gets approved, gets posted, and gets reimbursed. The tax component was never separated, because nobody asked for it and no field held it.


Once the claim is posted gross, the recoverable portion is not lost in principle — but recovering it requires going back to the receipt, extracting the tax, and adjusting the entry. Nobody does this retrospectively at volume. The tax is functionally gone at the moment the claim is posted without a split.


This is the single largest cause, and it is purely a data capture problem.


### 2. The evidence does not qualify


The employee attached something. Whether it qualifies is a different question.


Most jurisdictions require a proper tax invoice to support recovery — supplier name and tax registration number, date, description of the supply, tax-exclusive amount, rate, tax amount and total. Singapore’s[IRAS GST rules](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-%28gst%29) and the UK’s guidance on[VAT invoices and record keeping](https://www.gov.uk/vat-record-keeping/vat-invoices) both set out the minimum fields, with simplified rules below certain thresholds.


A credit card payment slip carries the merchant name, the amount and the last four digits of the card. It carries no tax registration number, no tax breakdown and no description of what was supplied. It is proof of payment, not proof of a taxable supply — and it supports no recovery at all.


Employees submit card slips constantly, because from their perspective it is a receipt. Unless the system tells them at submission that this particular document will not do, they will keep doing it, and the tax on every one of those claims is unrecoverable.


### 3. Conservative coding by default


This is the quietest failure and often the largest.


Faced with claims whose recoverability requires a judgement — is this client entertainment or a business meal? is this staff welfare or a benefit? — a finance team under time pressure adopts a safe default and codes the category as non-recoverable. It is defensible, it is fast, and it never produces an assessment.


It also forfeits recovery on a large volume of genuinely recoverable spend. And because the default is applied silently, nobody ever sees the cost of it. The alternative is not aggressive treatment; it is *per-claim* treatment driven by rules, so the judgement is made once when the rule is written rather than repeatedly under deadline pressure.

---


## What Is Actually Recoverable


The entitlement generally requires four things to hold simultaneously. All four, not any one.


**The expense was incurred for business purposes.** The personal portion of a mixed claim is not recoverable, which is one more reason attendee and purpose capture matters.


**The supplier was registered for the tax.** A small unregistered vendor charges no recoverable tax, whatever the receipt implies.


**The category is not blocked.** Every jurisdiction maintains a list of expenditure where input tax cannot be recovered regardless of business purpose — commonly certain client entertainment, private motor vehicle running costs, and benefits provided to employees or their families. The lists differ meaningfully between countries, which is why a multi-entity group cannot run one global rule.


**Valid evidence exists and is retained.** The tax invoice, kept for the statutory retention period, retrievable. Digital retention is accepted in most jurisdictions provided the copies are complete and legible, a position reflected in[AICPA and CIMA](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/) guidance on electronic records.


The important design point: **the employee paying personally does not break the entitlement.** Recovery follows the business purpose, not whose card was used. Organisations sometimes assume that out-of-pocket claims are outside the tax system entirely, which is wrong and expensive.


### Two cases worth calling out


**Per diem forfeits recovery.** A per diem allowance carries no recoverable input tax, because there is no tax invoice for the underlying spend. This is a genuine trade-off rather than a defect: per diem buys you the elimination of receipt handling and pays for it in forfeited tax. Before adopting per diem for a high-value category, quantify the tax you are giving up — we set out the broader comparison in[choosing between per diem and actual cost](https://peakflo.co/blog/travel-expense-policy-design-enforceable-rules) .


**Foreign tax is not domestic tax.** Tax charged in another jurisdiction generally cannot go in your domestic return. Some countries operate refund schemes for foreign businesses, each with its own evidence rules and deadlines. The minimum discipline is to code foreign tax distinctly rather than absorbing it silently into cost, so the decision to pursue a refund is at least available.


---


## Designing Recovery Into the Process


The fix is not a tax project. It is four changes to how claims are captured and coded.


### Extract the tax split at capture


The tax amount is printed on the receipt. If extraction reads merchant, date and gross amount, it can read the tax line too — and once that field exists, everything downstream becomes possible.


This depends entirely on extraction quality on real receipts, which is where template-based engines struggle most, because the tax line sits in a different position on every format. The connection between[receipt extraction accuracy](https://peakflo.co/blog/ai-ocr-expense-receipt-capture-energy-utilities) and tax recovery is direct and underappreciated: you cannot recover what you never captured.


### Validate the document type at submission


If the claim is in a category where recovery is available and the attached document looks like a card slip rather than a tax invoice, say so at submission — while the employee is still standing in the restaurant, not three weeks later.


This single intervention changes employee behaviour faster than any policy communication, because it makes the requirement concrete at the moment it can still be met. Asking for a tax invoice retrospectively almost never works.


### Encode the blocked list per entity


Recoverability by category is a rule, and rules belong in the system rather than in a person’s head. Each entity gets its own mapping of expense category to tax treatment, reflecting its own jurisdiction’s blocked list.


This is where the conservative-default problem gets solved: the judgement is made once, deliberately, when the rule is written and reviewed with your tax adviser — not repeatedly by whoever is clearing the queue on the last day of the month.


### Report recoverable tax as a number


What is not measured is not managed. A period report showing recoverable tax identified, recovered, blocked by category, and lost to invalid evidence turns an invisible leak into a tracked metric.


That last line is the useful one. Tax lost specifically because an employee submitted a card slip is a number that motivates change, and it belongs in the[T&E analytics](https://peakflo.co/blog/travel-expense-analytics-spend-visibility-finance-teams) pack alongside cost per trip and policy exception rate.


Tax treatment is also one of the eight dimensions a complete claim review should test, and it is the one most often skipped entirely — covered in our guide to[full-coverage expense audit](https://peakflo.co/blog/expense-report-audit-automation-full-coverage) .

## Our Verdict: How Much Attention Does This Deserve?


**Prioritise this if:**


- Your claims are posted gross with no tax split — this is the highest-value and easiest fix available
- You operate across multiple tax jurisdictions, where a single blocked-category rule is certainly wrong somewhere
- Finance applies a conservative default to categories requiring judgement, and nobody has sized what that costs
- Card slips are routinely accepted as receipts
- T&E volume is material, since recovery scales directly with it


**Lower priority if:**


- Your T&E spend is small relative to AP, where the same discipline applied to[supplier invoices](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable) returns considerably more
- You operate in a single jurisdiction with a simple regime and already split tax at capture
- Most of your T&E runs on per diem by deliberate policy choice, having already accepted the forfeited recovery


One caution. This is an area where getting it wrong in the other direction carries real cost — over-recovery produces assessments, interest and penalties. The blocked-category rules should be set with your tax adviser and reviewed when jurisdictions change them. The argument here is not for aggressive treatment; it is for *deliberate* treatment, replacing a silent default with an explicit rule. Professional guidance from bodies including the[ACCA](https://www.accaglobal.com/) and[IFAC](https://www.ifac.org/) consistently frames tax control the same way: a documented position applied consistently is defensible, and an undocumented habit is not.


---


## Conclusion


Input tax on employee expenses is unusual among finance improvements in that it returns cash rather than saved effort, and it is unusual among tax matters in that the obstacle is not complexity but data.


The tax was charged. The receipt shows it. The entitlement in most cases exists. What breaks the chain is that the claim gets posted gross, or the employee submitted a card slip, or somebody coded the category conservatively to avoid making a call. Three mundane failures, none of them requiring a tax specialist to fix.


Capture the split at the point of capture. Tell the employee at submission when their document will not support recovery. Encode the blocked list per entity so the judgement is made once. Then report the number, including what was lost and why.


Sample a quarter of your own claims and code them properly before deciding how much this matters. Most teams that run the exercise are surprised, and the surprise is rarely in the direction of it being smaller than expected.


---


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can you claim GST or VAT back on employee expense claims?


Yes, where the expense was incurred for business purposes, the supplier was registered, the category is not blocked, and a valid tax invoice supports the claim. The employee paying personally does not prevent recovery — the entitlement follows the business purpose, not who handed over the card.


### Why is input tax on expense claims so often unrecovered?


Three causes dominate: claims coded gross with no tax split, so the recoverable amount is never separated; card slips submitted instead of tax invoices, which fail the evidence test; and blanket conservative treatment where finance codes everything as non-recoverable to avoid assessing each claim.


### What makes a valid tax invoice for an expense claim?


Requirements vary by jurisdiction but generally include the supplier’s name and tax registration number, the date, a description of what was supplied, the tax-exclusive amount, the tax rate and amount, and the total. A card payment slip typically carries none of these and does not support recovery.


### What is blocked input tax on employee expenses?


Blocked input tax is tax that cannot be recovered regardless of business purpose or documentation. Commonly blocked categories include certain client entertainment, private motor vehicle costs, and benefits provided to employees or their families. The blocked list differs by jurisdiction and must be encoded per entity.


### How much input tax do companies typically fail to recover on T&E?


The loss is a function of T&E volume and tax rate rather than a fixed percentage. In practice the largest driver is not the blocked categories but the recoverable claims coded as non-recoverable by default, which can account for a substantial share of all claims where no per-claim assessment happens.


### Can you recover input tax on foreign travel expenses?


Generally not through your domestic return, because the tax was charged under another jurisdiction’s system. Some countries operate refund schemes for foreign businesses, with their own evidence and deadline requirements. Foreign tax should be coded distinctly rather than absorbed into cost silently.


### Should employees be asked to identify tax on their claims?


No. Claimants are not tax specialists and asking them to determine recoverability produces inconsistent data that finance must then re-check. The tax split should be extracted from the receipt automatically and the recoverability determined by rules based on category, entity and evidence type.


### How does per diem affect input tax recovery?


Per diem allowances generally carry no recoverable input tax, because no tax invoice exists for the underlying spend. This is a real trade-off: per diem removes receipt handling but forfeits recovery on those categories. Quantify the forfeited tax before choosing per diem for high-value categories.


### What records must be kept to support input tax recovery?


The valid tax invoice itself, retained for the statutory period, along with evidence of business purpose and the accounting entry showing how the tax was treated. Most jurisdictions accept digital copies provided they are complete, legible and retrievable for the full retention period.


### How do you start recovering input tax that is currently being missed?


Sample a quarter of historical claims and code each one properly to size the gap. Then fix it forward: extract the tax split at capture, encode the blocked list per entity, validate evidence type at submission, and report recoverable tax by period so the number becomes visible rather than assumed.
